opener.heading: Week 20: Backyard Science Lab 🔬
about: Seven days of experiments run in the yard out of the kitchen cupboard. She mixes her own bubble solution, cooks a cookie in a foil box with no plug, takes a dead flashlight apart on the table and follows a puddle until it has gone. Every day sets up a question in the morning and answers it before dinner, and most days leave something behind: a chalk line, a splinted stem, a drawing a meter wide.

No holiday lands this week, so the shape comes from the weather and from Thursday. Friday wants a bit of wind and Saturday wants sun, and the two will swap if May goes against you. On Day 140 Azlyn puts on one of Joseph's shirts, picks up a clipboard and runs three of the week's experiments back at you. Keep Friday's bubble mix and Monday's magnifier where you can find them again.
azlyn: Every hole makes a round bubble. Square, triangle, colander: the film pulls itself into the same shape each time.
The sun does work. A foil box, a sheet of black paper and eight cookies, with no plug anywhere in it.
Things come apart into parts. Spring, bulb, contact and switch out of a dead flashlight in order, one per hole of a muffin tin.
Symmetry she makes, then checks. Folded paint prints the second half, and the mirror tells her whether the two match.
Water leaves and comes back. A puddle dries off the paving by lunchtime and rains under plastic wrap in the afternoon.
you: Making the thing you use every day is a genuine revelation
Solar energy, demonstrated without a word of explanation
Careful observation is a skill, and it's mostly about slowing down
Symmetry is one of the first patterns children can produce as well as notice
Acting out a process beats being told it

A colander and a slotted spoon
A plastic bottle to cut the base off, and a second one for the magnifier
A clean sock you don't want back
A clean jam jar with its lid ring
A cardboard box with a lid (a pizza box or a shoebox)
A flattened cardboard box, or a length of lining paper
An empty box for the broken things
Chocolate buttons, or a bar to break up
A metal baking tray, and a second tray or a dishpan
A wooden spoon and a long spoon
A dish towel and two old towels
White school glue or a glue stick
A bar of soap and a little cooking oil
A muffin tin and a shallow tray
A sealable bag for the batteries
A dead flashlight, a broken clock or an expired battery toy
A magnifying glass, if you own one
Washable non-toxic poster paint in 3 colors

A hand mirror, or stiff card to cover with foil
Dried pasta shapes or building blocks
A large heatproof bowl and a plate
A watch or a phone timer
A clipboard, or stiff card and a clothespin
A sliced loaf of bread, butter and one filling
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 11 months this week. He stands on his own for a few seconds before he drops, pulls up on anything at his height, and copies the tune of your voice long before he copies the words in it.

days.title: Bubbles and Kites
days.prepTonight: Cut the base off a plastic bottle, pull a clean sock over the end, bend two pipe cleaners into a square and a triangle, and stand the lot by the back door with the straws, colander and spoon.

opening.title: The Bubble Mix That Has to Rest
opening.need: 1 liter warm water · 100 ml dish soap · 2 tbsp sugar · 1 lidded pitcher · 1 long spoon.
steps: She pours the warm water in, then the dish soap down the inside so it slides under the surface.
Sugar in. Stir slow with the spoon, ten turns, and stop. Fast stirring makes foam, and foam kills a big bubble.
Lid on, pitcher on the windowsill. It sits until 9:15.

main.title: Every Wand Makes a Round Bubble
materials: The rested bubble mix in a pitcher
1 plastic bottle with the base cut off (adult cuts) and a clean sock over the end
2 straws and a loop of string threaded between them
2 pipe cleaners, one bent into a square and one into a triangle
steps: Towel down on the paving, mix into the tray. Ask what shape a square hole makes and leave the answer alone.
A drinking straw each, hers snipped with a small hole near the top so she cannot suck the mix back up. Dip, blow gentle, and let her work until the first bubble comes off.
Slotted spoon next, then the colander, which makes forty at once and gets done twice. Then the square pipe cleaner and the triangle, and let her call the shape first.
The sock bottle: dip the sock end, blow through the neck, and a rope of foam comes out.
The jam jar lid ring for a clean circle. Then the two straws with the string loop, out on the grass: one in each hand, dip the whole loop, walk backwards. That one makes a bubble the size of her.
Back to the first question. Eight holes, a square and a triangle among them, and every bubble came out round.
main.tip: The sugar does glycerin's job, holding water in the film so it stretches further. A second batch works from the off.

outside.title: Reading the Wind with Bubbles
paras: Take the pitcher and one straw to the widest bit of the green. Blow a long run of bubbles tight against a wall, then out in the open, and mark the windier spot with a stone.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands on his own for a few seconds. Put him on the towel an arm's length back from the tray and blow bubbles above his head rather than at his face. He tracks one across, then studies the wet nothing on his palm.

second.title: The Grocery Bag Kite
second.intro: The bubbles found the wind. Now she builds something to send up into it.
materials: 2 garden stakes or straight sticks (substitute: 4 drinking straws taped end to end for a small one)
1 skewer or the scissor point, for piercing (adult)
Ribbon, or strips cut from a second bag
Her wind stone from this morning
steps: Cut the handles off and open the bag down both sides into one flat sheet. You cut, she smooths.
Lay the stakes in a cross, short one across the top third, and let her tape the joint with packing tape.
Tape all four stake ends to the plastic, then trim to a diamond a finger's width outside the frame.
Marker in her hand. Both sides are hers: names, faces, scribble.
Cut a meter of string for the tail, tape ribbon along it and tape it to the bottom point.
Pierce two holes either side of the joint, thread string through and knot a loop. Tie the flying line to the middle and unwind ten meters.
Out to her stone. She holds the line with both hands and you stand behind her, hands over hers.
second.tip: A kite that will not lift wants a longer tail rather than more running. Add an arm's length of ribbon and let the line out slowly.

alternatives: One bag, one stick, one string. It flies.
Windsocks from the same bag, taped to a stake in a pot.
Bubble ropes with the sock bottle, out on the grass.
outAgain: Grandparents or family, with the kite in the car
The green with the widest sky, if the wind holds
A friend's garden, because two kites beat one
The park, for the open half
A café with an outside table, if the wind drops

aroundWorld.title: China: The First Kites 🪁
paras: Kites flew over China two thousand years ago, built from silk and split bamboo. Armies used them to measure a river before building a bridge. Every spring the city of Weifang fills its sky with dragons and centipedes, some longer than a bus.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Cut her sandwich into a diamond with cucumber strips off one corner as the tail. Take the lunch out to the kite, the way Chinese families eat under theirs in spring.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: The Chinese word for kite, fengzheng, means wind harp.

days.krestonPM: Give him a sheet of parchment paper, the crackle without the risk. At 11 months the noise is the whole event and it holds him longer than any toy.

insight.headline: Making the thing you use every day is a genuine revelation.
paras: Bubble mix comes in a plastic bottle from a store, and until this morning that was where bubbles came from. Azlyn poured water, added soap and sugar, waited an hour and got the same thing out of a pitcher. Three-year-olds sort the world into things people make and things that arrive finished, and the second pile is enormous. Every time you move something across, she gets a piece of the world back. She will start asking where bread comes from, then socks, then rain. "Somebody made that" keeps her going a long way. Half of those answers you will have to look up.

days.safety: Soapy water turns paving into a skating rink, so keep the towel down, run the big string loop out on the grass, and rinse the slabs afterwards. The tray stays on a table or a step, never the floor. Kreston is 11 months. He cruises to anything at his height, and he will drink from it. Snip a small hole near the top of Azlyn's straw so the mix cannot come back up it, and keep her first practice blows away from the tray. Fly the kite clear of overhead wires and roads. Bag handles and offcuts go in the trash as you cut: plastic film over a face is fast and silent and Kreston is on the floor all afternoon. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Cooking Without Fire
days.prepTonight: Put a pizza box or a shoebox on the table with the foil, plastic wrap, black paper, masking tape and a wooden spoon. Check the forecast for sun.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Hottest Thing in the Garden

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: A Cool Bath After a Hot Day

opening.title: Lining the Box with Foil
opening.need: 1 cardboard box with a lid · kitchen foil · masking tape · 1 sheet black paper.
steps: Tear the foil into sheets she can handle and let her press them into the box, shiny side up, walls and floor. Creases are fine.
Tape the edges down, then line the underside of the lid the same way.
Black paper flat in the bottom, on the foil. Ask which holds more heat, the shiny bit or the black bit, and do not answer.

main.title: The Oven with No Plug
materials: 1 cardboard box with a lid (a pizza box or a shoebox)
1 sheet black paper or a dark plate
Chocolate buttons or a broken-up bar
A sunny step or table, and a watch
steps: Cut a square flap in the lid, one edge left uncut as a hinge. She stands back and you say why.
Tape plastic wrap tight across the hole underneath, so the box is sealed and she can see in.
Eight cookies on the metal tray, a pile of chocolate on each, tray into the box on the black paper.
Prop the flap open with the wooden spoon so it bounces sun down through the film. Carry the box to the sunny step and write the time on a strip of masking tape stuck to the lid.
Leave it alone. She checks the watch every fifteen minutes and reports back. Nothing happens for ages, then it all happens at once.
Once the chocolate goes glossy and slumps, lift the tray out with the dish towel and let her spread it with the spoon.
main.tip: The foil bounces light in, the black paper turns it into heat, the plastic wrap traps it. Say that once, in that order, while she is looking.

outside.title: The Hottest Thing in the Garden
paras: Mid-May sun has real heat in it by ten thirty. Go around the yard touching things with the back of her hand: a car hood, a paving slab in the sun, the same slab in shade, the fence, a metal gate. Get her to rank the top three, then check the box on the way past.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and sorting the sounds he hears from the ones he makes, so say hot the same way every time you mean it. Give him a square of foil taped over stiff card to bat at in the shade. It flashes and bends, and he will turn it over hunting for where the light went.

second.title: The Chalk Clock
second.intro: A stick, four stones and three colors of chalk turn the paving into a clock. She stands in the same spot three times over the afternoon and you draw round what the sun leaves.
materials: A sunny patch of paving or path
steps: Chalk a cross on the paving big enough for both her feet. She stands on it facing the same way each time.
Draw round her shadow in the first color while she holds still. Arms out makes it easier for you and funnier for her.
Stand the stick upright a step away, wedged with the four stones, and chalk along its shadow in the same color.
Set the timer for 35 minutes and go and do something else.
Timer goes: back on the cross, second color, round her shadow and the stick's shadow again.
Third round after another 35 minutes, third color. She notices the change before you point at it.
Look at all three together. Ask which shadow is longest and which way they are swinging.
second.tip: She will move on the cross, every time. Chalk round her feet on the first go and line her toes up to those marks every round after.

alternatives: Chalk one shadow, hers, and leave the stick out of it.
Shadow shapes with her hands on a sunlit wall.
Race three things melting on the step: butter, chocolate, an ice cube.
outAgain: The fire station, or wherever the tractors are working this month
A drive past the field being cut, windows down
The park with the most shade
The garden center, cool inside and full of things to look at
The kiddie pool on the lawn, if the heat has held
days.krestonPM: Kreston comes with whatever you pick. Back home before dinner, sit him on a shaded patch of paving and chalk round him where he sits. At 11 months a sitting outline is the one you will get, and Azlyn will want to draw it. Keep him off hot paving in bare feet, and offer him water more often than her.

insight.headline: Solar energy, demonstrated without a word of explanation.
paras: Azlyn ate a cookie that the sun cooked. No plug, no flame, no switch, and she watched it happen through a window of plastic wrap. She has no framework for energy yet and does not need one. She has a memory of the sun doing work, and that memory is what the word solar will attach itself to in a classroom in four years' time. Concepts land better on top of an experience than on top of a definition. Your job today was carrying the box to the sunny step and then keeping quiet about it. She will ask for the box again on the next hot morning, and the answer is yes.

days.safety: The foil box and the metal tray get hot in direct sun, so you lift the tray out with the dish towel and she waits. Sun on both children through the middle of the day: sunscreen before you go out and again after lunch, hats, shade, water. Kreston overheats faster than Azlyn and cannot tell you, so check the back of his neck and never leave him in direct sun. A kiddie pool holds enough water to drown an 11-month-old, so stay inside arm's reach of Kreston every second it holds water and tip it out onto the grass before you come in. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Broken and Fixed
days.prepTonight: Empty a box for her to fill in the morning, get the glue, tapes, string and bulldog clip on the table, and hide the dead flashlight until the afternoon.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Book She Taped Back Together

opening.title: Hunting the Broken Things
opening.need: 1 empty box · paper and a marker · the shelf where broken things go.
steps: Hand her the box and walk the house top to bottom, including the shelf of things you meant to deal with in March.
Three rules: it has to be broken, it has to fit in the box, and it cannot be anybody's favorite.
Sit down with the paper and write what each one is and what is wrong with it, in her words.

main.title: The Fix-It Bench
materials: The box of broken things she collected
White school glue or a glue stick
A bar of soap and a little cooking oil
steps: Lay them out in a row, worst first. Pick three to mend for real, the rest go back in the box.
Torn page or card: masking tape along the back of the tear, her thumbs pressing from the middle out. Damp cloth for sticky fingers.
Snapped plastic or wood: white school glue on both faces, wrap string round twice, clamp the bulldog clip on. Packing tape round a split handle where glue will not hold.
Stuck rather than broken gets a different fix: a bar of soap rubbed down a sticking zipper, a drop of oil in a squeaking hinge. She works each one back and forth until it moves.
Loose screw on a chair or a hinge: you drive the screwdriver, she puts her hand over yours to feel it go tight.
Back to the list. Write FIXED beside the ones that are, and a reason beside the ones that are not.
main.tip: Let her hand you each item and say what is wrong before you touch it. Naming the break is most of the diagnosis.

outside.title: Splinting the Floppy Plants
paras: Walk the garden looking for anything bent, snapped or leaning: a broken stem, a top-heavy plant in a pot. Mid-May growth is soft and fast, and something is always flopping. Splint what is mendable with a short stick and a wrap of masking tape, loose enough to grow into.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a few seconds, which puts his hands at table height for the first time. Everything on the fix-it bench is in reach. Give him his own job on the floor a good way off: a cardboard box with a flap he can open and shut.

second.title: Inside the Broken Flashlight
second.intro: She has never seen the inside of anything in this house. One dead thing comes apart on the table this afternoon.
materials: 1 dead flashlight, broken clock or expired battery toy
1 old toothbrush for the dusty bits
steps: Batteries out first, before anything else opens. Into the sealable bag, zipped, onto a high shelf. She watches you do it and hears why.
You turn the screws, she holds the flashlight steady, and every screw goes into the first hole of the muffin tin.
Take it apart in order, one part per hole, left to right. Name each piece as you lift it: spring, bulb, contact, switch, case.
Old toothbrush over the dusty parts. She does the brushing.
Ask which piece she thinks made the light, then hold the bulb up to the window for her to look into.
Paper and marker: she draws each part in its own square while you write her name for it rather than the real one.
Screw it back together as far as it will go, or leave it in the tin on a high shelf for tomorrow.
second.tip: Go slow enough that she can predict the next piece. Ask what she thinks is under the bit you are about to lift.

alternatives: Take apart a click pen instead, five parts and no tools.
Sort the button jar into a muffin tin by size.
Draw the inside of the flashlight on one big sheet instead of squares.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, and count this week's ducklings
A long walk with the stroller, wherever it goes
Round the block hunting for things being mended: scaffolding, a van with its hood up
The green with a ball, if the afternoon has gone loud
days.krestonPM: At the pond he will point at the ducks, and pointing at 11 months is a whole sentence, so say the word back every time. He may hand you a stone, take it back, then hand it over again, which is the game. Keep him in your arms at the water's edge, every second.

insight.headline: Repair teaches something disposal can't.
paras: A broken thing thrown out teaches Azlyn that objects are disposable and that adults have no power over them. A broken thing mended on the kitchen table teaches her that the world is made of parts, that parts go back together, and that she is allowed to try. Watch how she treats the next broken thing in this house now that she has seen you have a go at four. The mend does not have to be pretty or permanent, and tape on a book spine counts. She leaves today knowing that broken and finished are two different words, and she will point out the mended spine every time that book comes off the shelf.

days.safety: Screwdrivers, springs and loose screws go back in the tin between uses, and a flashlight bulb breaks into glass, so the bulb is yours to hold. Batteries come out and into a sealed bag on a high shelf before anything else happens. A swallowed button battery burns through a child from the inside within hours and is an ambulance, not a wait-and-see. Kreston is cruising and everything on that table is at his height. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Small Things, Close Up
days.prepTonight: Wash a jam jar and stand it upside down to dry with the plastic wrap, an elastic band and a shallow tray beside it. Find the magnifying glass if you own one.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Ten Things Smaller Than Her Thumb

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Slowest Lap of the Garden

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Leaf as Big as the Paper

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Water Drop Jar and a Cookie

opening.title: Ten Things Smaller Than Her Thumb
opening.need: 1 shallow tray · her thumb · the house and the garden.
steps: Hold your thumb up and give her the one rule: into the tray if it is smaller than her thumb.
Let her hunt: a seed, a crumb of moss, a bit of eggshell, a button, a bead, a torn corner of leaf. Ten is the target and eight is fine.
Lay them in a line across the tray, biggest to smallest, and ask which she wants first. That one goes under the drop at 9:15.

main.title: The Water Drop Magnifier
materials: 1 clean jam jar or a plastic bottle with the top cut off (adult cuts)
The tray of ten small things
A real magnifying glass, if you own one
steps: Stretch plastic wrap over the jar mouth and hold it with the elastic band round the neck. Push the middle down so it dips.
One teaspoon, one fat drop into the dip. One. She will want to flood it, so let her do a second jar rather than a second drop.
Dark paper flat on the table, jar standing on it, her first small thing sliding underneath. Look down through the drop.
Her turn, and it takes a minute. Show her how to move her head up and down until the thing snaps into focus, then leave her.
Work through the tray. Then the back of her own hand under the jar, the one she calls you over for.
Paper and crayons: she draws one thing at the size she saw it rather than the size it is. If you own a magnifying glass, hold it over the same thing for her to look through and compare.
main.tip: A flat drop has picked up dust or soap. Tip it off, dry the film with your sleeve and put a fresh one on.

outside.title: The Slowest Lap of the Garden
paras: One lap of the garden, twenty minutes, no destination. One rule, out loud: you both stop at anything either of you notices. May turns the garden over fast, so expect aphids on a rose stem, a spider on the fence, a bud that was shut on Friday. Count the stops and tell her the number at the gate.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and works the opposite way, mouthing things to find out about them. That makes the tray of ten small things a choking tray, so it lives above his head all day. Sit him on the grass with one big smooth stone instead, the same investigation at his size.

second.title: The Leaf as Big as the Paper
second.intro: One leaf, drawn a meter wide, every vein getting a line of its own. It takes an afternoon and she will not want to stop.
materials: 1 flattened cardboard box or a length of lining paper
1 second sheet of paper for you
A plastic bottle with the top cut off, plastic wrap and an elastic band, for floor work
steps: Tape the flattened box to the floor at all four corners so it cannot slide under her hand.
She picks the leaf, whatever the shape, and one is enough.
Look at it through the drop first, both of you: the thick vein up the middle, the thin ones coming off it.
Pencil: the outline, a meter across. Start it if she asks, then hand the pencil over.
The thick middle vein next, in one crayon color, stalk to tip.
Then the branching ones, one at a time, back to the drop each time she loses her place.
Hold the real leaf against the drawing at the end and let her tell you what she put in that she cannot see standing up.
second.tip: Sit on the floor and draw your own leaf on a second sheet rather than watching hers. She works longer beside someone working than beside someone supervising.

alternatives: Rub the leaf through paper with the side of a crayon and stop there.
Draw her own thumbprint the size of a plate.
Line up ten leaves smallest to biggest and tape them down.
outAgain: The green with a ball, and let her kick it as far as she can
The playing field, for running in a straight line after an afternoon on the floor
A walk to look at other people's gardens
The riverside path with the stroller, as far as she will walk
days.krestonPM: Out on the grass Kreston will stand himself up against the stroller, let go, and hold for a couple of seconds before he drops. Roll the ball to him where he sits. At 11 months he pushes it back with both hands rather than throwing it, the start of a game he and Azlyn will play for years.

insight.headline: Careful observation is a skill, and it's mostly about slowing down.
paras: Azlyn can see a leaf. Staying with one for a quarter of an hour is a different thing, and it is trainable. The water drop worked this morning because it forced her to hold still, keep her head at one distance, and stay with one object long enough for the detail to arrive. Attention builds through practice on something worth attending to, and ten good minutes on a Monday is a real result at three. The slow lap of the garden did the same job with no equipment at all. Expect her to stop you on the path for the rest of the week.

days.safety: A real glass magnifying lens left on a sunny windowsill or carried outside will focus the sun and scorch paper, carpet and skin within seconds. It stays indoors, on the table, with you. The tray of ten small things is choking-sized, all of it, so it goes up high the moment you walk away from it. The afternoon drawing happens on the floor, so cut the top off a plastic bottle and make the drop in that for floor work, or leave the jam jar standing on the table and carry the leaf over to it. Glass at floor height and an eleven-month-old pulling himself up do not share a room.

days.title: Two Halves That Match
days.prepTonight: Newspaper over the table, ten sheets of thin paper on top of it, the three paints, three teaspoons and the clothespins beside them. Swim bag by the door.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Folding the Paper Down the Middle

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Half a Thing in the Mirror

opening.title: Folding the Paper Down the Middle
opening.need: thin paper, 10 sheets · 1 marker · the table.
steps: Show her one fold: corner onto corner, hold them together, then press the crease flat with a thumbnail from the middle out.
She folds the other nine. They will not all match at the corners, which does not matter today.
Number the backs 1 to 10 with the marker and stack them folded. Tell her the paint goes on one side only.

main.title: The Paint That Copies Itself
materials: Thin paper, 10 sheets, folded in half
Clothespins and a line, or a radiator
steps: Newspaper down, one folded sheet opened flat in front of her. Paint on one side of the crease only, a teaspoon per color, blobs rather than stripes.
Before she folds it, ask what will be on the empty half. Take her answer as it comes and do not correct it.
Fold, then press with both flat hands from the crease outward. Open it.
Washcloth for her hands, then the next sheet. Nine to go and she will speed up.
Change one thing each time: one color, then three, then a long blob crossing the crease, then a blob sitting right on it.
Clip them along the line or lay them on the radiator, and write her name for each on the back in marker. She will call most of them butterfly.
main.tip: The blob that sits on the crease is the one worth doing twice. It prints into itself and comes out as one shape rather than two.

outside.title: Leaves With Two Matching Sides
paras: Hunt for leaves that fold onto themselves. Most do, and she tests each by folding it down the middle vein to see whether the edges land together. May hedges are full of fresh soft leaves that fold without snapping. Collect the ones that match and one that does not.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and bangs two things together to hear what they do, which matches this morning if you hand him the right pair: two wooden spoons, or two plastic lids. Sit him on the newspaper at the far end while Azlyn prints, and name the colors out loud, because he takes in far more of it than he gives back.

second.title: Half a Thing in the Mirror
second.intro: A mirror stood upright on a fold line finishes a drawing she has only half made. She will move it back and forth before she believes it.
materials: 1 hand mirror (substitute: stiff card covered in kitchen foil, taped at the back)
steps: Draw half a face down the fold of a sheet: one eye, half a nose, half a mouth. Stand the mirror on the line and let her look into it.
Her turn to draw half of something, her choice, and she stands the mirror on the line herself.
Run a strip of masking tape down the middle of the table. She lays pasta shapes or blocks along one side of it.
She copies that row onto the other side, one piece at a time, matching the distances by eye.
Stand the mirror on the tape and check. Anything out of place shows up at once.
Move one piece while she is not looking and let her find it with the mirror. Then she moves one and you find it.
Bring out this morning's dried prints and stand the mirror down the crease of each. Crayons for the ones she wants colored, both halves matching.
second.tip: She may hold the mirror flat and be baffled. Show her the upright position once, then let her go back to experimenting. The flat mirror is worth her time too.

alternatives: Fold and cut paper snowflakes and open them out.
Build a tower, then build its twin beside it.
Lay her hands flat either side of the tape and look at those.
outAgain: Swimming
The splash pad, if the pool is booked out
Indoor playground, if it has rained all afternoon
The park on the way home, twenty minutes and no more
Home for a long bath instead, on the weeks nobody has it in them
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool too. At 11 months he can sit on the shallow step with your hands on him and slap the water flat-palmed for as long as you let him. Twenty minutes is his limit before he goes cold. Hold him facing you at first so the noise arrives with your face in front of him.

insight.headline: Symmetry is one of the first patterns children can produce as well as notice.
paras: Azlyn has been reading symmetry since she was a few months old, because faces are symmetrical and babies stare at faces. Producing it is newer. Folding paint gave her a way to make a symmetrical thing without the hand control that drawing one would demand, and the mirror let her check her own work without you telling her whether it was right. That loop, make it and test it, is the part she keeps. Expect butterflies, faces and hearts in her drawing for weeks, and expect her to fold things in half to see what happens. Hand her the mirror when she asks whether one of them came out right, rather than the answer.

days.safety: A glass hand mirror on the floor with an 11-month-old who stands up and drops things is a bad combination. Keep it at the table with her, put it away between turns, and give Kreston the foil-card version if he wants one. Dry pasta shapes are choking-sized, so sweep them off the floor before he goes down. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Water Comes Back
days.prepTonight: Fill the ice cube tray and put it in the freezer. Chalk, bucket, measuring pitcher, the wide paintbrush and an old towel by the back door.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Chalk Line Round the Water

opening.title: The Chalk Line Round the Water
opening.need: sidewalk chalk · 1 bucket of water · 1 wide paintbrush.
steps: Out on the paving in pajamas if that is where you are. She dips the brush and paints one wet patch the size of a plate.
Chalk round the edge of it while it is still shiny, as close as she can get.
Go in and have breakfast. Come back out at 9:15 and look at the line. Say nothing and let her tell you.

main.title: Where the Puddle Goes
steps: Find two dry spots on the same paving, one in full sun and one in shade. Check both with a hand first.
Fill the pitcher from the bucket to the same line twice, and let her pour one puddle on each spot, slow, so they spread rather than run off.
Chalk round each one straight away, a different color for each. Those are the starting lines.
Timer on for fifteen minutes. Every time it goes, both of you out with the chalk for a fresh line round each puddle.
Keep going until the sunny one has gone. Count the rings inside each color and let her tell you which puddle worked harder.
Towel down for wet knees. Once the waiting bores her, hand her the brush and the bucket to race her own wet lines against the sun.
main.tip: Do not tell her where the water went. Ask her, write down the answer at half past ten, and read it back at four o'clock.

outside.title: Following the Downpipe
paras: Follow the water off the house. Start at the gutter, trace the downpipe to the ground and find the grate it disappears into. Pour a pitcher of water in the top and get her down at the bottom listening for it to arrive. Then walk the street and find where the road tips toward the drains, because somebody built that slope on purpose.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and pouring is the game he would pick if he could ask for it. Give him a shallow tray with a centimeter of water and two plastic cups, sat down, with you next to him. Never leave him with it, not for a moment, and tip it out when you move on.

second.title: Rain Under the Plastic Wrap
second.intro: The puddle vanished this morning without going anywhere she could see. The same water goes up and comes back down this afternoon, in a bowl on the table.
materials: Hot water from the tap (adult pours)
steps: Bowl on the plate at the back of the table, well past her reach. You pour the hot tap water in, a third full, and she stands back and hears why.
Plastic wrap across the top, pressed down all round the rim so no steam escapes.
Spoon in the middle of the film so it sags into a shallow cone over the water.
She stays in her chair and hands you the six ice cubes one at a time. You set them on the film around the spoon. Then both of you watch from the side.
Drops gather on the underside, run down the slope to the dip and fall back into the bowl. Ask her where that water came from.
Paper and marker: draw it as a circle. Water in the bowl, up as steam, drops on the film, back down. She draws the arrows, you write her words.
Peel the film back once it has cooled, tip the ice in, then empty the bowl into the sink together.
second.tip: She will want the ice on top before the film is sealed. Hold the order, because the seal is what makes it work.

alternatives: Ice cubes on a plate in the sun, timed against ice cubes in the fridge.
Paint the fence with water and watch the marks go.
Breathe on a cold window and draw in it.
outAgain: The indoor play center, and let her go until she stops
Indoor playground, if the play center is full of a party
The park, if the afternoon has turned out fine
A puddle walk in rain boots, if it has rained since lunch
days.krestonPM: At the play center he goes in the under-ones area and stays there. At 11 months he pulls up on the padded blocks, stands, and lets go to see what happens, and soft flooring is the best place to practice that. Twenty minutes on his own patch before anything else.

insight.headline: Cycles are harder than sequences.
paras: Azlyn handles a sequence with no trouble, because breakfast comes before shoes and shoes come before the door. A cycle has no beginning, and that is the hard part. She will want to know where the water starts. Today gave her a loop she could stand next to and watch go round twice, which is worth more than a diagram of one. Expect her to get it wrong for a while, and to use it in odd places, like asking whether her bath water becomes rain. Answer that one with a yes, because it is the right answer. She runs the loop back at you in her own words for a week, and the version she settles on is hers.

days.safety: Hot tap water scalds a three-year-old at temperatures that feel fine on your hands, so you pour it and the bowl stays at the back of the table. The bucket, the bowl and Kreston's water tray get emptied the moment you finish. Kreston is 11 months and can drown in a few centimeters of water, and he does it in silence, so he is never alone with any of it.

days.title: Azlyn Runs the Lab
days.prepTonight: Hang one of Joseph's white shirts on her chair with two safety pins, put the goggles and clipboard on top, and check there is bread in.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Jars, Washed and Lined Up

opening.title: Sleeves Rolled and Pinned
opening.need: 1 of Joseph's white shirts · 2 safety pins · swim goggles · 1 clipboard or stiff card with a clothespin · paper and a marker.
steps: Shirt on over her clothes, sleeves rolled to her wrists and pinned. It hangs to her ankles, which is the correct look.
Goggles up on her forehead, ready to come down when she needs them.
Clipboard, paper, marker. She writes her name on the top sheet however it comes out, you write LAB underneath and hand it back.

main.title: The Three Stations
materials: 1 of Joseph's white shirts, sleeves rolled and pinned
1 clipboard, or stiff card with a clothespin on it
The bubble mix and one wand
The water drop magnifier and the tray of small things
1 teaspoon and a little water, to refill the magnifier's dip
The mirror or foil card and the half-drawings
steps: Three spaces along the table, one per station: bubble mix and wand, magnifier and the tray of small things, mirror and half-drawings. Monday's drop has dried out, so a fresh teaspoon of water goes into the dip first.
She decorates the three signs while you write the words she gives you. Signs go up behind their stations.
Station one is hers to run, shirt on and goggles down. You are the visitor. Do what she tells you, and do it wrong when her instruction is wrong.
Station two the same. She hands you the magnifier, puts a small thing under it and tells you where to put your eye.
Station three: she stands the mirror on the fold line and asks you the question she was asked twice this week.
Between stations she marks the clipboard for everything you got right. She decides what counts.
main.tip: Say "I don't know, you're the scientist" and mean it. The gaps in her version beat a correction from you.

outside.title: Checking on the Week's Experiments
paras: A walk around the yard with the clipboard, looking at what the week left outside. The chalk clock lines, faded and rained on. Sunday's splinted plants, and whether they took. The two puddle spots, dry now. Finish where the kite went up.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and hands things over on purpose now, then waits for you to take them. Give him a station at the end of the table: a plastic tub and three big wooden spoons to post in and tip out. Azlyn will want to run his station too, so let her.

second.title: The Sandwich Line
second.intro: Three chairs, three jobs, one loaf. She does every job in turn and finds which one holds the line up.
steps: Three chairs in a line, one board at each. Job one is two slices out of the bag. Job two is butter, with the knife. Job three is filling on, top slice on, cut across, onto the tray.
She takes job one, you take job two, job three goes to whoever else is in the house or to you.
Run one sandwich down the line before anybody talks about it.
Swap. She takes job two and you take job one. Run another.
Swap again so she has done all three. Let the buttering be slow.
Ask which job was hardest and which was fastest, and whether the line ran better with nobody waiting.
Wrap them in parchment paper and stack them on the tray. Those are tomorrow's lunch.
second.tip: Let the line jam. Butter slower than she can deal slices out for one round and let her watch the bread pile up. She will tell you to hurry up.

alternatives: One job each and no swapping, on a long day.
A line for folding and stacking the clean dish towels instead.
Let her make one sandwich start to finish, no line at all.
outAgain: The post office, and she hands the parcel over herself
The corner store for milk, with a coin she hands over at the register
The park on the way back, if the line was short
The green with the ball, for a last run before dinner
days.krestonPM: Take him into the post office in the carrier facing out. At 11 months the line, the noise and the strangers are work for him. He buries his face in your shoulder when it gets to be too much, which is him regulating himself. Back home he gets a crust with his tea.

insight.headline: Acting out a process beats being told it.
paras: Azlyn ran three experiments this morning and told you how each one worked. Explaining a thing out loud forces her to put it in order, notice the gaps and fill them, which is why she got more from ten minutes of teaching you than from an hour of being taught. Teachers call it the protégé effect and it works on adults too. The sandwich line did the same with her body, standing her inside the process rather than describing it. Hand her the running of things more often than feels efficient. It costs you time and buys her the whole shape of a task.

days.safety: The butter knife lives in your hand between jobs and goes back out of reach the moment the line stops, and she uses it sitting down with you beside her. Count the two safety pins into her cuffs in the morning and count them out at bath time, because Kreston finds a dropped pin before you do. Nothing glass goes on his end of the table, so his posting station is a plastic tub and the week's jars stay up at Azlyn's end.
